entries.claim: The bad loop count is caused by a use-after-free: the memory was released and handed to another object.
entries.evidence: The writers are sub_001F7930 iterating a list and updating each element via MEM32(esi + 8) - a field, not an object base. Nothing was freed. investigate.py's classifier asserted this and was wrong.

entries.claim: Skipping the dispatch loop is free, because every call in it targets 0 and fails, so the loop achieves nothing.
entries.evidence: Measured 1452 -> 56 kernel calls against an unchanged seed list. 'Every call fails' is not 'the loop has no effect' - it still advances an index and the failing calls run through the safe stub, which touches esp and eax.

entries.claim: The 16-byte allocation is failing and returning null.
entries.evidence: The allocation site is a clean operator-new plus constructor and it succeeds; 0x030FEFE8 is a legitimately allocated buffer.

entries.claim: esp escaping the 8 MB stack means the stack is corrupted.
entries.evidence: 0x03DAB1C8 is the worker thread's own stack, allocated from guest heap by PsCreateSystemThreadEx. triage_crash's heuristic does not model the second thread.
Written once by sub_00239E50+0x15C, before the loop that reads it.

entries.claim: The boot is deterministic, so a single run is a sound measurement.
entries.evidence: The three gated counters repeat exactly, but total dispatch volume swings 8x between runs (622M vs 74.9M). Stable where the gate looks; not stable in general.

entries.claim: kernel_calls is an adequate progress signal.
entries.evidence: It read exactly 1452 across 566 seeded functions, 31 lifter repairs and a fixed freeze. It saturates where the boot stops. Replaced as the primary gate by `reached` (distinct dispatch targets), first measurement 692.

entries.claim: A missing function is what blocks the boot.
entries.evidence: 566 functions that vtables provably call were seeded and measured safe; kernel_calls did not move. Worth re-testing against `reached`, which did not exist at the time.

entries.claim: iteration-cap gets the boot past spin@sub_001F7930->0x00000000
entries.evidence: applied at sub_001F7930: capped loop back-edge to loc_001F7964 at recomp_0014.c:38840. reached/kernel_calls did not rise (2144 -> 2144), reverted.

entries.claim: iteration-cap gets the boot past spin@sub_001F7930->0x00000000
entries.evidence: applied at sub_001F7930: capped loop back-edge to loc_001F7964 at recomp_0014.c:38840. reached/kernel_calls did not rise (2144 -> 2144), reverted.

entries.claim: The loop's count field is an end-pointer of a begin/end range over an array of function pointers
entries.evidence: Measured the memory the pointers bracket: MEM32(0x00F81180)=0x00F84600 (back-pointer to the object), +4=0x00F812B0, +8=0x00F81188 (self-pointer). Heap pointers, not code addresses. Not a function-pointer array.

entries.claim: registry+0x2C is maintained as a linked-list head by sub_0019FBC7 but read as an {array,count} descriptor by the loop in sub_001F7930
entries.evidence: Object at 0x00F84600 = {0x00F812B0, 0x00F81180, 0, 0}; the memory it points to contains a self-pointer (0x00F81188 -> itself) and a back-pointer to the object - the classic empty-list sentinel shape. sub_0019FBC7 does list splicing (MEM32(ecx)=esi; MEM32(edx)=ecx; MEM32(esi+4)=ecx) and is the writer of that pointer. BOTH functions are faithfully lifted per faithful.py, so neither side is a translation bug. Open fork: whether sub_0019FBC7 legitimately owns that field, or has a wrong pointer.

entries.claim: registry+0x28 and +0x2C are one embedded list head, so the loop reads half of a two-word structure
entries.evidence: Dumped registry+0x24..+0x30 at loop entry: +0x24=0, +0x28=0, +0x2C=0x00F84600, +0x30=0x00F81288. +0x28 is zero, so it is not the other half of a list head. Note +0x30 holds the registry's OWN base address - a self-reference not yet explained.

entries.claim: sub_0019FBC7 is game code maintaining a linked list, and registry+0x2C is either its list head or its victim
entries.evidence: Call stack proves sub_0019FBC7 is the HEAP ALLOCATOR's internal list manager: sub_0019FBC7 <- sub_001A0B0C <- sub_003437C7 <- sub_003437F3 (operator new) <- sub_00216251 <- sub_00236500 <- sub_00239E50. It is free-list bookkeeping, not game logic.

entries.claim: The heap allocator writes its own free-list links INSIDE the registry's live memory block
entries.evidence: Probe at the splice site fired with eax=0x00F81358, node=0x00F81360, registry base (MEM32(0x5BC508))=0x00F81288, offset=0xD0. So a node was spliced at registry+0xD8 while the registry pointer was already set. Either the registry block was freed and returned to the free list, or the allocator's bookkeeping is writing out of bounds. Not yet distinguished - do not act on this until it is.

entries.claim: The engine allocator (sub_003437F3) returns the SAME address for multiple distinct allocations
entries.evidence: Direct measurement with a duplicate detector on every return: 7 allocations, 4 distinct, 3 duplicates. 0x00F81288 was returned on allocations #3, #4 and #6 as well as its first. So several live objects occupy one block and overwrite each other. This is the root cause of the registry's fields holding heap pointers, the free-list links found inside it, and the bogus 16-million count - all of them are other objects' data in the same memory.

entries.claim: Probes and logging calls inserted into generated code are behaviourally free
entries.evidence: Adding recomp_alloc_log/recomp_alloc_fixup calls at the allocator's return in sub_003437F3 made the boot die at 33 kernel calls in 2 of 3 runs. Removing them: 5 of 5 runs at 692/1452/152/11, exactly stable. Causation established by removal. The allocator return is not a safe place to call out to C - likely stdio locking or timing, since stdio locks have deadlocked this boot before.

entries.claim: The 7-allocations/3-duplicates measurement describes the clean boot
entries.evidence: That measurement was taken WITH the allocator instrumentation in place, and the instrumentation is now proven to perturb the boot (2 of 3 runs died early). The duplicate returns are a direct observation so they are probably real, but the count and ordering were recorded on a disturbed system and must be re-measured without perturbing the allocator before anything is built on them.
